Analyst tools: predictions, residuals and validation

Source: vignettes/brs-analyst-tools.Rmd
brs-analyst-tools.Rmd

This vignette shows the post-estimation tools for brs() fits: predictions on the mean and score scales, contrasts with standard errors, marginal effects, residuals, plots, the parametric bootstrap, cross-validation and summary tables. The model itself is described in vignette("brs-intro"); the mixed-model versions of these tools are in vignette("brs-mm"). Small numbers of replicates and folds keep the vignette fast, so the results are illustrative.

library(betaregscale)

Data and fit

Simulated NRS-11 scores of 240 patients at three post-operative times, with age and a treatment indicator:

set.seed(2023)
nrs <- data.frame(
  time = factor(rep(c("6h", "12h", "24h"), each = 80),
                levels = c("6h", "12h", "24h")),
  age = round(rnorm(240, 50, 12)),
  trt = rbinom(240, 1, 0.5)
)
nrs$age_c <- (nrs$age - 50) / 10
eta <- -0.6 + c(0, 0.5, -0.3)[nrs$time] + 0.2 * nrs$age_c - 0.5 * nrs$trt
shp <- brs_repar(mu = plogis(eta), phi = 0.2, repar = 2)
nrs$y <- round(10 * rbeta(240, shp$shape1, shp$shape2))

fit <- brs(y ~ time + age_c + trt, data = nrs, ncuts = 10)
fit
#> 
#> Call:
#> brs(formula = y ~ time + age_c + trt, data = nrs, ncuts = 10)
#> 
#> Coefficients (mean model with logit link):
#> (Intercept)     time12h     time24h       age_c         trt 
#>     -0.4574      0.2262     -0.6128      0.1310     -0.3633 
#> 
#> Coefficients (dispersion model for sigma with logit link):
#>   (phi) 
#> -1.2626

Predictions

predict() returns, by type:

type value
"response" (default) the mean E(Y)=μE(Y) = \mu on (0,1)(0, 1)
"link" the linear predictor of the mean
"precision" the second parameter on its own scale (the dispersion σ\sigma under repar = 2)
"variance" Var(Y)\mathrm{Var}(Y)
"quantile" quantiles of YY at the probabilities at
"score" the latent score at E(Y)E(Y) (KE(Y)K\,E(Y) under "mid")
"expected_score" the expected recorded score ∑ssP(S=s)\sum_s s\,P(S = s) 
nd <- data.frame(time = c("6h", "12h", "24h"), age_c = 0, trt = 0)
cbind(nd,
      mu = predict(fit, nd),
      score = predict(fit, nd, type = "score"),
      expected_score = predict(fit, nd, type = "expected_score"))
#>   time age_c trt        mu    score expected_score
#> 1   6h     0   0 0.3875968 3.875968       3.873384
#> 2  12h     0   0 0.4424592 4.424592       4.423637
#> 3  24h     0   0 0.2553673 2.553673       2.539366
predict(fit, nd, type = "quantile", at = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))
#>          q_0.25     q_0.5    q_0.75
#> [1,] 0.19959732 0.3644270 0.5557468
#> [2,] 0.25391890 0.4305352 0.6207733
#> [3,] 0.08600763 0.2067570 0.3832926

brs_predict_scoreprob() gives the probability of each score, as a matrix or in long format:

round(brs_predict_scoreprob(fit, newdata = nd), 3)
#>      score_0 score_1 score_2 score_3 score_4 score_5 score_6 score_7 score_8
#> [1,]   0.042   0.134   0.152   0.151   0.141   0.124   0.102   0.077   0.051
#> [2,]   0.023   0.095   0.127   0.140   0.142   0.135   0.121   0.100   0.072
#> [3,]   0.158   0.235   0.180   0.139   0.105   0.076   0.052   0.032   0.017
#>      score_9 score_10
#> [1,]   0.024    0.003
#> [2,]   0.039    0.005
#> [3,]   0.005    0.000
head(brs_predict_scoreprob(fit, newdata = nd, scores = 0:2, format = "long"))
#>   id score       prob
#> 1  1     0 0.04181922
#> 2  1     1 0.13358466
#> 3  1     2 0.15198673
#> 4  2     0 0.02250122
#> 5  2     1 0.09524590
#> 6  2     2 0.12691577

Score-scale quantities with standard errors

brs_marginal() returns score probabilities (type = "prob"), expected scores ("expected_score") or exceedance probabilities P(S≥k)P(S \ge k) ("exceed") with delta-method standard errors and Wald intervals, computed on the logit scale for probabilities and expected scores so they stay in range (contrasts use Wald intervals on the natural scale). contrast gives differences between pairs of rows of newdata; c(i, j) is row i minus row j:

brs_marginal(fit, nd, type = "exceed", k = 4)
#>   time age_c trt row k  estimate  std.error     lower     upper
#> 1   6h     0   0   1 4 0.5211590 0.05244215 0.4189245 0.6216513
#> 2  12h     0   0   2 4 0.6149118 0.05076843 0.5119463 0.7085225
#> 3  24h     0   0   3 4 0.2885185 0.04173023 0.2139919 0.3765655
brs_marginal(fit, nd, type = "expected_score",
             contrast = rbind(c(2, 1), c(3, 1)))
#>   contrast row1 row2   estimate std.error      lower      upper
#> 1    2 - 1    2    1  0.5502529 0.3675773 -0.1701853  1.2706912
#> 2    3 - 1    3    1 -1.3340178 0.3497652 -2.0195451 -0.6484905

With se_method = "simulation", the standard errors and percentile intervals come from n_sim draws of the parameters (set a seed first):

set.seed(1)
brs_marginal(fit, nd[1:2, ], type = "expected_score", contrast = c(2, 1),
             se_method = "simulation", n_sim = 200)
#>   contrast row1 row2  estimate std.error      lower    upper
#> 1    2 - 1    2    1 0.5502529 0.3636081 -0.1616128 1.275677

Average marginal effects

brs_marginaleffects() gives the average marginal effect of each numeric covariate on the mean (type = "response") or on the linear predictor ("link"): a central difference for continuous covariates and the discrete change for 0/1 covariates, averaged over the rows. Intervals use n_sim draws from the asymptotic normal law of the estimates. Factors are not included; code a factor as 0/1 dummies to get its contrast, or use brs_marginal() contrasts as above.

set.seed(2)
ame <- brs_marginaleffects(fit, n_sim = 100, keep_draws = TRUE)
ame
#>   variable         ame  std.error     ci.lower    ci.upper model     type   n
#> 1    age_c  0.02778234 0.01051475  0.007953519  0.05177403  mean response 240
#> 2      trt -0.07703774 0.02756216 -0.137031764 -0.02828654  mean response 240

Effects on E(Y)E(Y) are on (0,1)(0, 1); multiply by KK for the score scale under "mid".

autoplot.brs_marginaleffects(ame, type = "forest")

Residuals

residuals() offers the types below. The randomized quantile residuals ("rqr", Dunn and Smyth, 1996) are standard normal under the model whatever the censoring and are the recommended type for diagnostics.

type definition
"response" (default) yt minus the fitted mean
"pearson" response residual over the fitted SD
"deviance" beta deviance residual at yt
"rqr" Φ−1(ui)\Phi^{-1}(u_i), uiu_i uniform on (F(li),F(ui))(F(l_i), F(u_i)), with 0 and 1 at the borders
"weighted", "sweighted" residuals on the logit(Y)\mathrm{logit}(Y) scale (Espinheira et al., 2008)
"cell_deviance" signi−2log⁡Pi\mathrm{sign}_i\sqrt{-2\log P_i} from the probability of the observed cell

All types except "rqr" and "cell_deviance" use one point of the cell, yt: s/Ks/K under "mid" (so the border scores sit at 10−510^{-5} and 1−10−51 - 10^{-5}) and the cell center under "right"/"left". They are unreliable at the border scores. The cell deviance residuals are signed by the observed minus the expected score; for score data their squares add up to −2log⁡L-2\log L:

set.seed(1)
r_q <- residuals(fit, type = "rqr")
c(mean = mean(r_q), sd = sd(r_q))
#>      mean        sd 
#> 0.0026605 0.9873903
r_d <- residuals(fit, type = "cell_deviance")
c(sum_sq = sum(r_d^2), minus2logLik = -2 * as.numeric(logLik(fit)))
#>       sum_sq minus2logLik 
#>     997.6295     997.6295

Plots

plot() draws up to six diagnostic panels of quantile residuals (four by default) in base graphics or, with gg = TRUE, ggplot2:

plot(fit, gg = TRUE)

autoplot.brs() adds a calibration plot, the predicted score distribution, fitted CDFs and residuals by censoring type:

autoplot.brs(fit, type = "calibration")

autoplot.brs(fit, type = "score_dist")

brs_cens() summarizes the censoring types of a fit:

brs_cens(fit, gg = TRUE)

Parametric bootstrap

brs_bootstrap() draws new responses at the fitted shapes, re-coarsens them on the fit’s cells and refits the original formula, R times. It returns percentile, basic, normal or BCa intervals next to the Wald intervals; failed refits are counted and printed. Use R of at least 199 in practice; 49 is used here for speed.

set.seed(3)
boot <- brs_bootstrap(fit, R = 49, keep_draws = TRUE)
boot
#> Bootstrap confidence intervals
#>   Level: 0.95 | CI: percentile | Successful replicates: 49 / 49 | Attempts: 49 
#>   Failed replicates: 0 (0.0% of attempts)
#> 
#>     parameter   estimate    se_boot    ci_lower   ci_upper  mcse_lower
#> 1 (Intercept) -0.4574253 0.10590803 -0.62188294 -0.2784529 0.014002540
#> 2     time12h  0.2262380 0.13772964 -0.01369944  0.4354400 0.021238725
#> 3     time24h -0.6127630 0.14066571 -0.86158613 -0.3400873 0.042576014
#> 4       age_c  0.1310349 0.05142949  0.03795532  0.2162490 0.009765608
#> 5         trt -0.3632532 0.13790026 -0.61820543 -0.1155792 0.034133318
#> 6       (phi) -1.2625569 0.08818543 -1.42443996 -1.0969682 0.014821331
#>    mcse_upper  wald_lower wald_upper level
#> 1 0.039331473 -0.70499315 -0.2098574  0.95
#> 2 0.021264852 -0.07056248  0.5230386  0.95
#> 3 0.024659678 -0.92888949 -0.2966365  0.95
#> 4 0.007618617  0.02425109  0.2378187  0.95
#> 5 0.030051529 -0.61610640 -0.1103999  0.95
#> 6 0.031921649 -1.44051168 -1.0846021  0.95
autoplot.brs_bootstrap(boot, type = "ci_forest")

Cross-validation

brs_cv() runs repeated k-fold cross-validation. For each held-out fold it reports log_score, the mean log probability of the held-out observations (higher is better), and the RMSE and MAE of yt around the predicted mean:

set.seed(4)
cv_full <- brs_cv(y ~ time + age_c + trt, data = nrs, k = 5, ncuts = 10)
set.seed(4)
cv_time <- brs_cv(y ~ time, data = nrs, k = 5, ncuts = 10)
cv_full
#>   repeat fold n_train n_test log_score   rmse_yt    mae_yt converged error
#> 1      1    1     192     48 -2.028631 0.2001736 0.1618597      TRUE  <NA>
#> 2      1    2     192     48 -2.168236 0.2422893 0.2152613      TRUE  <NA>
#> 3      1    3     192     48 -2.185514 0.2470601 0.2150859      TRUE  <NA>
#> 4      1    4     192     48 -2.076509 0.2360192 0.1934935      TRUE  <NA>
#> 5      1    5     192     48 -2.040262 0.2026502 0.1702655      TRUE  <NA>
c(full = mean(cv_full$log_score), time_only = mean(cv_time$log_score))
#>      full time_only 
#> -2.099831 -2.122464

Resetting the seed gives both models the same folds.

Tables

brs_est() gives the coefficient table, brs_gof() the fit criteria and brs_table() a comparison of several fits with their censoring counts:

brs_est(fit)
#>      variable   estimate         se    z_value      p_value    ci_lower
#> 1 (Intercept) -0.4574253 0.12631247  -3.621379 2.930372e-04 -0.70499315
#> 2     time12h  0.2262380 0.15143162   1.493995 1.351770e-01 -0.07056248
#> 3     time24h -0.6127630 0.16129199  -3.799091 1.452277e-04 -0.92888949
#> 4       age_c  0.1310349 0.05448253   2.405081 1.616889e-02  0.02425109
#> 5         trt -0.3632532 0.12900912  -2.815717 4.866855e-03 -0.61610640
#> 6       (phi) -1.2625569 0.09079493 -13.905588 5.858308e-44 -1.44051168
#>     ci_upper
#> 1 -0.2098574
#> 2  0.5230386
#> 3 -0.2966365
#> 4  0.2378187
#> 5 -0.1103999
#> 6 -1.0846021
fit_time <- brs(y ~ time, data = nrs, ncuts = 10)
brs_table(full = fit, time_only = fit_time, sort_by = "AIC")
#>       model nobs npar    logLik      AIC      BIC pseudo_r2 exact left right
#> 1      full  240    6 -498.8148 1009.630 1030.513    0.1668     0   24     0
#> 2 time_only  240    4 -506.3028 1020.606 1034.528    0.1013     0   24     0
#>   interval prop_exact prop_left prop_right prop_interval
#> 1      216          0       0.1          0           0.9
#> 2      216          0       0.1          0           0.9
